items.question: If CSS Modules scopes a class name locally, can a global reset or a third-party selector still affect the element?
items.answer: Yes. CSS Modules transform module class and animation names, but the resulting CSS still participates in the normal cascade. Global selectors, inherited properties, resets, inline styles, and third-party rules can still matter.
items.trap: The naive answer treats local naming as DOM or cascade isolation. It is only a build-time naming boundary, not Shadow DOM-style encapsulation.

items.question: Does adopting Tailwind utilities by itself create a design system?
items.answer: No. Tailwind theme variables can define reusable values and generate utilities, but a design system also needs semantic component APIs, accessibility decisions, documentation, governance, and validation.
items.trap: The naive answer equates a styling vocabulary with a complete product and component system. Utilities do not define behavior, ownership, or accessible states.

items.question: Why can a custom property value appear valid when declared, yet make a consuming declaration fall back to its initial or inherited value?
items.answer: Double-dash custom properties accept almost any token sequence when parsed. The browser substitutes the value at computed-value time; if that result is invalid for the consuming property, the consuming property uses its initial or inherited value. Typed `@property` registration can constrain the custom property.
items.trap: The naive answer assumes custom properties are type-checked like ordinary CSS properties at declaration time.

items.question: Why is a stored `dark` or `light` value not the same thing as the resolved theme?
items.answer: A user preference can be explicit or `system`. Only the system preference should follow `prefers-color-scheme`; an explicit choice must win even if the operating system changes. The resolved attribute or class is what CSS consumes.
items.trap: The naive answer overwrites the user's explicit choice whenever the OS preference changes, making the preference model impossible to reason about.

items.question: Does `color-scheme` replace the need to define dark and light component colors?
items.answer: No. `color-scheme` tells the user agent which schemes an element supports so browser-provided UI can adapt. Component authors still need media-query or selector-driven rules, or an equivalent color strategy, for their authored content.
items.trap: The naive answer confuses browser UI adaptation with author stylesheet theming.

items.question: Is CSS-in-JS automatically safer for SSR because styles are colocated with components?
items.answer: No. Colocation is an authoring benefit, not an SSR guarantee. The chosen engine must be evaluated for server rendering, streaming, style ordering, runtime work, extraction behavior, and CSP constraints.
items.trap: The naive answer treats a programming model as proof of a rendering and deployment property.

items.question: Why is documenting an internal class name usually a weaker customization API than documenting a slot or semantic variant?
items.answer: Internal selectors couple consumers to DOM structure and implementation details. A semantic variant or slot can remain stable while the markup and styling engine change, and it can be tested alongside behavior and accessibility.
items.trap: The naive answer optimizes for immediate CSS power while ignoring upgrade compatibility and the component's behavioral contract.

items.question: Can a highly specific selector in a normal cascade layer always override a less specific unlayered author rule?
items.answer: No. Cascade origin and layer precedence are considered before specificity. Normal unlayered author styles outrank normal layered author styles, so specificity inside the lower-precedence layer cannot rescue the declaration.
items.trap: The naive answer starts with specificity and skips the earlier cascade steps.

items.question: Does declaring layers solve every override problem?
items.answer: No. Layers make one part of ordering explicit, but origin, importance, specificity, scoping proximity, inheritance, and source order still matter. Layering also requires a clear ownership and import policy.
items.trap: The naive answer treats `@layer` as a universal replacement for understanding the cascade.

items.question: Why should a component usually consume semantic tokens rather than a primitive token such as a raw blue value?
items.answer: Semantic tokens express roles such as action or surface. A brand or color-mode theme can then replace the value behind the same role without making components branch on brand or mode. Primitive tokens remain useful as the source scale.
items.trap: The naive answer treats token indirection as needless naming instead of the mechanism that decouples component intent from palette implementation.

items.question: Can a visual change be breaking even when every TypeScript prop still compiles?
items.answer: Yes. The public contract includes documented visual behavior, tokens, styling hooks, accessibility behavior, and interaction expectations. A layout, contrast, or interaction change can require consumer action even when the type surface is unchanged.
items.trap: The naive answer defines compatibility only as type-checking, missing runtime and visual contracts.

items.question: Why is sharing a generated application stylesheet a tighter coupling than sharing a Tailwind theme package?
items.answer: A generated stylesheet embeds an application's complete output and build assumptions. A theme package can publish the token contract as importable CSS, allowing each consumer to compile the utilities and composition it needs against its own application.
items.trap: The naive answer assumes sharing more compiled CSS necessarily means better reuse; it can instead create hidden ordering and version dependencies.

items.question: Why is replacing the styling engine under a stable component boundary safer than rewriting every consumer at once?
items.answer: Consumers depend on the stable component contract rather than generated class names or engine-specific calls. An adapter and incremental migration can preserve behavior while teams move independently, with SSR and visual checks catching differences.
items.trap: The naive answer assumes a flag-day rewrite is simpler because it removes temporary adapters, ignoring coordination and regression risk.

items.question: Is a large number of published components evidence that a design system is successful?
items.answer: Not by itself. A design system is a product with adoption, support, upgrade, accessibility, and quality outcomes. Useful measures include duplication reduction, upgrade success, issue resolution, and regressions, not component count alone.
items.trap: The naive answer rewards inventory growth even when consumers cannot safely adopt or maintain the system.

mcqs.question: Which statement best describes CSS custom properties declared with the `--name` syntax?
options: They are substituted at build time and are absent from delivered CSS.
They participate in the cascade and inherit by default.
They can be used as CSS property names inside `var()`.
They are automatically type-checked as colors, lengths, or numbers.
mcqs.explanation: Double-dash custom properties are part of the browser CSS model, so they cascade and inherit by default. Option 0 describes typical preprocessor substitution, option 2 misstates where `var()` is valid, and option 3 ignores that unregistered custom properties are not automatically typed.

mcqs.question: A normal author rule in `@layer app` conflicts with a normal unlayered author rule. Which normally has higher precedence?
options: The layered rule, because layers always override unlayered CSS.
The rule with the more specific selector, regardless of layer.
The unlayered rule, before specificity is compared.
The rule that appears first in the source.
mcqs.explanation: For normal author declarations, unlayered styles outrank layered styles, so the cascade can discard the layered candidate before specificity. The best distractor is option 1: specificity matters only after origin and layer precedence are tied.

mcqs.question: What is the role of `color-scheme: light dark`?
options: It automatically rewrites every authored color in the document.
It declares that the element can be rendered in both schemes and lets user-agent UI adapt.
It permanently selects dark mode even when the user prefers light.
It replaces `prefers-color-scheme` for authored component styles.
mcqs.explanation: `color-scheme` advertises supported schemes and lets browser UI such as controls and scrollbars adapt. Authored content still needs its own theme rules, commonly using `prefers-color-scheme` or a selector. Option 0 is the most plausible misconception: the property does not rewrite arbitrary authored colors.

mcqs.question: A theme preference is `system`, and the OS changes from light to dark. What should happen?
options: The resolved theme should follow the new OS preference.
The preference should be permanently changed to `dark`.
The app should ignore the OS after the first render.
The app should always choose light because it is the safe default.
mcqs.explanation: `system` means the resolved theme follows the current `prefers-color-scheme` result, so a media-query change should update the resolved state. Option 1 confuses a resolved value with the stored preference.

mcqs.question: Which is the strongest public styling contract for a reusable Button?
options: Consumers must target the generated `.css-8f2a` class.
Consumers may depend on the component's current nested `<span>` structure.
Consumers use documented variants, sizes, states, and deliberate slots.
Consumers copy the component stylesheet and edit it locally.
mcqs.explanation: Semantic variants, states, and slots describe intentional API surface and can survive internal markup or engine changes. Options 0 and 1 couple consumers to implementation details; option 3 forks the system instead of creating a supported extension point.

mcqs.question: What is the main reason to separate primitive and semantic design tokens?
options: To make components depend directly on raw palette values.
To let themes replace role-based values without component brand branches.
To prevent aliases from being used in token files.
To ensure every component has a unique color scale.
mcqs.explanation: Primitive tokens provide a scale; semantic tokens express roles consumed by components. Themes can change the mapped values while preserving the role contract. Option 0 reverses the goal, while options 2 and 3 are not requirements of a token hierarchy.

mcqs.question: Under SemVer, removing a documented token that consumers use is normally what kind of release for a stable package?
options: A patch release, because tokens are implementation details.
A minor release, because removal is a form of deprecation.
A major release, because it is an incompatible public API change.
No release is needed if TypeScript still compiles.
mcqs.explanation: A documented token is part of the public contract; removing it is backward-incompatible and therefore calls for a major version under SemVer. Deprecation is a migration step, not a classification that makes removal minor.

mcqs.question: What is a practical reason to publish a shared Tailwind theme as importable CSS?
options: Each consumer can compile its own utilities from a shared token contract.
It forces every application to ship identical generated CSS.
It removes the need for versioning or migration notes.
It makes application-specific composition global by default.
mcqs.explanation: Tailwind theme variables are defined in CSS and can be imported by multiple projects, allowing each build to use the shared values while retaining local composition. Option 1 is the coupling the package is meant to avoid; token sharing does not remove governance.

mcqs.question: Which evaluation is most important when choosing a runtime CSS-in-JS engine for an SSR component library?
options: Whether it makes every selector globally unique, regardless of output.
Whether its rendering, extraction, ordering, CSP, and runtime costs fit the targets.
Whether it eliminates the need for semantic component APIs.
Whether it guarantees zero CSS bytes in the browser.
mcqs.explanation: The choice should be measured against server rendering or streaming, style ordering, runtime work, extraction, browser output, CSP, and consumer interoperability. The other options promise properties no styling engine can usefully guarantee and ignore the library contract.

mcqs.question: Which metric is a stronger design-system operating signal than the number of components published?
options: The number of internal selectors per component.
The number of components that have never been adopted.
Consumer upgrade success and accessibility regression rate.
The amount of generated CSS regardless of usage.
mcqs.explanation: Upgrade success and accessibility regressions test whether the system delivers safe, useful outcomes for consumers. Component count, unused inventory, selector count, and raw CSS volume can grow without adoption or quality.

scenarios.prompt: A server-rendered app supports `light`, `dark`, and `system`, but users see a light flash before dark mode appears and hydration sometimes changes the page. Repair the theme bootstrap and explain the preference/resolved-theme boundary.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Keep the stored value as the preference, including `system`; do not treat the resolved value as the persisted setting. Run equivalent, defensive bootstrap logic in an inline head script or on the server before the first paint, and set the same `data-theme` contract used by CSS. On the client, reconcile the preference and subscribe to `MediaQueryList` changes only while the preference is `system`; explicit light or dark must win. Avoid reading `localStorage` unguarded during SSR, and make the server and client initial attribute agree to prevent hydration mismatch. Add `color-scheme` and test first paint, OS changes, explicit overrides, forced colors, and storage failures.
rubric: Separates stored preference from resolved theme and preserves explicit overrides.
Bootstraps the attribute or class before paint and keeps server/client output consistent.
Uses `matchMedia` changes only for the system preference and handles SSR safely.
Accounts for browser UI via `color-scheme` and tests accessibility and failure cases.

scenarios.prompt: A vendor stylesheet wins over your component styles despite a more specific component selector. Establish a predictable layer policy without using routine `!important` overrides.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Declare the layer order in the application entry point and import the vendor sheet into a deliberately low layer, for example `@layer reset, tokens, vendor, components, utilities, app;` followed by `@import url('vendor.css') layer(vendor);`. Keep the component selector shallow and give component and application layers clear ownership. A normal unlayered or later higher-precedence layer can then win without escalating specificity. Verify the actual production import order, because bundler concatenation can change assumptions. Do not claim that `:where()` alone solves precedence: it intentionally contributes zero specificity, so layer placement and ownership are the primary controls.
rubric: Uses an explicit layer order and demotes third-party CSS into a controlled layer.
Explains that layer precedence is evaluated before specificity for normal declarations.
Avoids routine `!important` and keeps selectors shallow and maintainable.
Checks production bundling and validates representative conflicts.

scenarios.prompt: You are migrating a large runtime CSS-in-JS component library. Consumers currently rely on generated class names, while the target is static CSS plus custom properties. Propose an incremental boundary and identify what must be tested.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Freeze new use of the runtime API and first inventory generated-class consumers, theme reads, SSR ordering, and public styling hooks. Preserve `Button` as the stable boundary, map semantic `tone` and `size` to stable attributes or documented classes, and move values into a versioned custom-property contract. Implement the new static implementation behind the same component API, retaining an adapter for consumers that cannot migrate immediately. Migrate low-risk components first and compare server and client markup and styles. Run visual regression across variants, states, themes, and responsive cases; test focus and accessibility behavior; and measure representative bundle and render costs before and after. Deprecate generated selectors rather than making them a new contract.
rubric: Preserves a stable semantic component API and introduces a token/custom-property contract.
Uses adapters and phased migration instead of a flag-day rewrite.
Audits generated-class consumers and verifies SSR/client ordering and markup.
Covers visual, theme, state, accessibility, and performance regression tests.
Provides deprecation and migration guidance for implementation-dependent consumers.
